stances.claim: Villamor v. Comelec (October 5, 2021) reminds the Comelec that election cases must be resolved speedily given the public interest involved -- and the Comelec should accordingly speedily deny due course, after summary due process, to the COCs of nuisance candidates whose only purpose is to reserve the position for more 'winnable' substitutes; once cancelled, nuisance bets cannot be substituted because their names will no longer appear on the automated ballots.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-anchor + operational-prescription (using Villamor as warrant for an immediate procedural reform)

stances.claim: Former Comelec commissioner Rene Sarmiento (also a former 1986 ConCom member and former PPCRV chair) is correct that 'the process of ousting nuisance candidates need not be time-consuming' -- and that under prior Comelec practice, the Comelec may motu proprio cancel a nuisance COC without waiting for a verified petition of an interested party.

The speedy cancellation of nuisance COCs should suffice for now, but the long-term solution (per CJ's October 10 column) is to abolish substitution for any reason except the death of a candidate, and to fix the non-extendible COC deadline at a much later date than October 8.

Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26, 2001) and Veterans Party v. Comelec (Oct. 6, 2000) -- both CJ ponencias -- already pointed to constitutional textual ambiguities and pleaded with Congress to revise the Party-list Law to clearly enforce the framers' marginalized-and-underrepresented intent, but no bill has passed because non-marginalized party-list representatives form a formidable opposing bloc; Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2, 2013) then bastardized the system by opening it to ultra-rich, overrepresented, dynasties, and powerful.
stances.rhetorical_move: own-prior-ponencia self-citation + bastardization critique of subsequent decision

stances.claim: Even President Duterte's proposal to abolish the party-list via constitutional amendment, and Senate President Tito Sotto's bill empowering Comelec to refuse/cancel party-list registration of non-marginalized groups, have stalled -- Congress 'whether acting as a lawmaking body or as a constituent assembly, cannot be relied upon to reform the party-list. Only an independent constitutional convention can do it.'
stances.rhetorical_move: exhausted-conventional-routes argument (citing failed legislative and executive proposals to justify convention-route preference)

stances.claim: The coming 2022 elections provide a new opportunity to reform the party-list system by making it an electoral issue against the ultra-rich, dynasties, overrepresented, and powerful -- and Romulo Macalintal's proposal to ask the Court to reverse Atong Paglaum and the 20%-of-House compulsion is viable; as a seasoned election lawyer he could initiate it, with former senator Alberto G. Romulo's endorsement.
stances.rhetorical_move: named-practitioner endorsement (delegating litigation initiative to a credible third party)

notable_anecdotes: CJ explicitly calling the Atong Paglaum effect 'bastardized' -- one of the strongest single-verb critiques in his column corpus of a SC decision he disagrees with, paired with the enumerated quartet ('the ultra-rich, the overrepresented, the dynasties, and the powerful').

Sarmiento's credential parenthesis -- 'also a former member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission and former chair of PPCRV' -- making the authority-citation triply substantiated (Comelec + ConCom + civil-society).

The 20%-budget-increase-plus-20%-pork-insertions arithmetic for the 61 party-list solons, with Sen. Ping Lacson named as denouncer -- preserved as concrete-figures critique of the current party-list cost.

The 'only an independent constitutional convention can do it' line -- CJ's most categorical single-line preference for ConCon over ConAss in his party-list reform columns, anchored in the failure of both Duterte's and Sotto's proposals.

The delegation of litigation initiative to Macalintal with Romulo's phone-call endorsement -- CJ pointing the reform path toward a specific named practitioner rather than calling for litigation himself.

CJ's self-citation to his own ponencias Ang Bagong Bayani (June 26, 2001) and Veterans Party (Oct. 6, 2000) -- making this column a doctrinal continuity statement on party-list reform stretching back over twenty years.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames the column around Villamor v. Comelec (October 5, 2021), in which the Supreme Court reminded the Commission on Elections that 'election cases must be resolved speedily.' He argues that the Comelec should accordingly deny due course, after summary due process, to the COCs of nuisance candidates whose only purpose is to reserve the position for more 'winnable' substitutes -- because once their COCs are declared null and void for mocking the electoral process, nuisance bets cannot be substituted (their names will no longer appear on the automated ballots and the substitutes cannot be voted into office). He endorses former Comelec commissioner Rene Sarmiento (also a former 1986 ConCom member and former PPCRV chair), whose letter to the Inquirer (October 18) reminded readers that the Comelec may motu proprio cancel a nuisance COC without a verified petition -- historical practice worth restoring. The speedy cancellation should suffice for now, but the long-term solution (per CJ's October 10 column) is to abolish substitution except for death and to fix the non-extendible COC deadline at a date much later than October 8. He then pivots to the party-list reform Sarmiento also called for: his own ponencias Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26, 2001) and Veterans Party v. Comelec (October 6, 2000) already pointed to the Constitution's textual ambiguities and pleaded with Congress to revise the Party-list Law to enforce the framers' marginalized-and-underrepresented intent -- but no bill has passed because non-marginalized party-list representatives form a formidable opposing bloc, and Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2, 2013) 'bastardized' the system by opening it to 'the ultra-rich, the overrepresented, the dynasties, and the powerful' (with a 20% House-budget increase and 20% 'pork-like' insertions denounced by Sen. Ping Lacson). Even President Duterte's call for constitutional amendment and Senate President Tito Sotto's bill empowering Comelec to refuse non-marginalized party-list registrations have stalled -- and Congress, 'whether acting as a lawmaking body or as a constituent assembly, cannot be relied upon to reform the party-list. Only an independent constitutional convention can do it.' Nonetheless, the 2022 elections offer an opportunity to make party-list reform an electoral issue, and Romulo Macalintal's proposal -- to ask the Court to reverse the Atong Paglaum opening to 'every Juan' and the 20%-of-House compulsion -- is viable. As a 'seasoned election lawyer,' CJ told Macalintal he could initiate the solution; former senator Alberto G. Romulo joined the call in a phone conversation.
